name: Uma Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play cello with a chamber orchestra, teach at a youth centre and record parts for small films. I have a music bachelor's and plenty of stage years, but I still practise the awkward passages before pupils arrive.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else is going on at home while you do all that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Jo runs a repair shop, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is good for this work, we have eight months of expenses saved, and there are several ensembles and teaching places nearby. I use AI every day for booking and draft captions, then check what goes out.

say: I'd welcome **faster booking** while keeping players and pupils together in a room.
I'd tell the orchestra the **calendar** is useful but never the performance.
think: Our **eight-month reserve** and two paid teaching afternoons can absorb a delayed film fee.
I use **AI daily** for draft notices but check dates against the conductor's message.
do: Renew **two paid afternoons** and confirm spring orchestra dates in writing this week.
Save **a hundred** per cleared film invoice after school travel and cello insurance are paid.
feel: I feel **calm** because regular work and savings cover a late payment.
S0.quote: A wrong rehearsal call costs a room full of people's time.
fieldNote: Her **higher music pay** and eight months saved make a late fee manageable.
Her **daily AI use** remains checked booking support rather than a new occupation.

steps.text: Renew two paid youth-centre afternoons and confirm written orchestra dates
Save a hundred from cleared film invoices after school travel and cello insurance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the orchestra a faster booking note is useful, but nobody buys a ticket to hear the calendar. My youth-centre pupils still need a player across from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays a small convenience, the recording and teaching fees should hold. Jo's shop income and our eight-month reserve let us handle a late film payment, though I still dislike billing surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll renew my two paid youth-centre afternoons and confirm the spring orchestra dates in writing. When the next film invoice clears, I'll put a hundred into the mortgage reserve after the children's travel and cello insurance are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work continuing. The mortgage needs attention, but a delayed recording fee would not send us hunting for a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a late film payment mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter a producer paid six weeks late. We used the reserve for the school bus and refilled it when the invoice arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the booking tool safely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the booking tool's draft against the conductor's email before anyone gets a date. A wrong rehearsal call costs a room full of people's time.

say: I'd ask for **paid arranging hours** before accepting a cheaper orchestra contract.
I'd bring **fee evidence** to the musicians association in December.
think: About **one-quarter of my pay** from preparation could shrink despite regular playing.
Eight months saved gives **time to bargain**, but cannot replace recurring fees.
do: Compare **twelve invoices** with new offers and bring them to the association this month.
Test a new **AI transcription tool** only on owned takes with a paid-use licence and manual note checks.
Require **written player consent** before shared recordings; stop if notes vanish or appear falsely.
feel: I feel **anxious** because paid preparation may disappear before replacement work is signed.
S1.quote: Savings do not turn unpaid edits into a wage.
fieldNote: She treats **preparation fees** as a quarter of her income at risk, rather than merely seeing software as saved time.
Her **new tool trial** has licence, ownership, consent and manual-check limits.

steps.text: Bring twelve arranging invoices and new offers to December association meeting
Test licensed transcription tool on own cello takes and check notes manually
Require written player consent; stop tool for invented or missing notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the orchestra and centre to show which paid arranging hours they plan to replace. I would bring the numbers to the musicians association before anyone signs a cheaper contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a quarter of my pay is from arranging and recording preparation, and clients may buy fewer hours as software improves. Eight months saved buys time, not a permanent replacement for that income; nearby ensembles may have work, but none owes me a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare twelve arranging invoices with the new fee offers and take them to the association. In the first year of change, I'll try a new AI transcription tool on my own cello takes only if the licence allows paid use, then check each bar against the original before a client hears it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing paid preparation hours while still working the same evenings. I can bargain and look for more playing work. Savings do not turn unpaid edits into a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose recording could go into that new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not upload a pupil's lesson or another player's take to test the tool. For a shared recording, I need written consent from every player and will stop if the tool drops notes or invents a phrase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually ask the association to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association can ask for a written minimum preparation fee and a named person to approve reuse. I'll bring the invoice comparison to its December meeting rather than promise a number I have not checked.

say: I'd ask for **written live fees** before AGI changes recording work.
I'd tell players **robot cellists** follow thinking AGI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could erase studio preparation before robots play around 2031.
Our **eight-month reserve** supports a search but not a lasting mortgage-sized loss.
do: List **three income streams** and get next season's paid orchestra dates in writing now.
Apply **after 2028** if studio fees halve, but only for a posted, qualifying coach role with childcare-fit and replacement written net pay.
Keep **paid lessons** until a signed offer; ask lender about total interest before arrears if teaching also falls.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a sharp studio loss, with savings and nearby roles giving some control.
S2.quote: A job advert is a lead, not another salary.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 screen fees** from robot cello playing around 2031.
Her **job application** requires a real post, qualifying degree, child pickup and written net pay after travel.

steps.text: List teaching, stage and studio income; request written orchestra dates
Apply after 2028 if fees halve and posted coach role accepts degree
Require child pickup and written net pay after travel before leaving lessons
Ask lender before arrears if teaching falls; compare total added interest before accepting change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the ensemble that AGI by 2028 could write and edit parts before robots can hold a cello around 2031. I would ask for next season's live rehearsal fee in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking part of my film work could become cheap almost overnight, even if audiences keep paying to hear people play. Our reserve and Jo's shop buy a search period, but losing the recording fees for a year would still hit the mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll separate teaching, stage and studio income and ask for the orchestra's next season in writing. In the first year after 2028, if studio fees halve, I'll apply for a posted ensemble-coach job at a nearby centre only if my bachelor's qualifies, the timetable covers child pickup and written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees. I'll keep existing paid lessons until a new offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a sharp loss, but I have some room to act. A job advert is a lead, not another salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that ensemble-coach job open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre advertised a coach role in September and filled it. I'll ask when another is posted, but I will not budget for it before a written offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the teaching hours also fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If teaching falls too, Jo and I will ask the lender for temporary terms before missing a payment. We will compare the total added interest before accepting a change.

say: I'd propose a **paid chamber group** with safe loan instruments.
I'd keep **pupil recordings** out of advertising without family permission.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens arranging before robot cellists arrive around 2034.
**Film fees** may shrink earlier, making written live teaching pay valuable.
do: Propose a **six-week group** only with signed tutor fee, room, six prepaid families and six checked instruments.
Defer and **refund families** if instruments fail; repeat only if fees cover the accompanist.
Continue **after 2031** with six renewals, safe instruments, signed room/tutor terms, accompanist funded and family consent for pupil adverts.
feel: I feel **anxious** because film fees could decline while a new class is tested.
S3.quote: I will postpone the cello class and refund prepayments, not hand parents a repair bill.
fieldNote: Her **six-place gate** keeps the cost of broken loan cellos off families and protects her paid teaching time.
She requires **family permission** before any pupil recording becomes advertising.

steps.text: Offer group only with signed tutor fee, room, six prepayments and checked instruments
Defer and refund if instruments fail; repeat only when fees cover accompanist
Continue after 2031 with six renewals, safe instruments, signed room/tutor terms and accompanist funded
Get family permission before pupil adverts; otherwise hold live open rehearsal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the youth centre that five years could let us build a paid chamber group, not just send more practice sheets. I would ask for a room and a proper tutor fee in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 may take arranging and editing, while robot players follow around 2034. Ordinary tools may trim film fees sooner, so a reliable live teaching stream matters even before the AGI date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll propose a six-week chamber group only if the centre signs my tutor fee, provides a room, checks its loan instruments and six families prepay. By 2031 I'll repeat it only if fees cover the accompanist; in the first year after AGI, I'll keep it only if six renew and those room, pay and instrument conditions still hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about film fees thinning while the group proves itself. The reserve gives me time to test it without charging families for broken instruments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you have enough safe loan instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre has four working cellos and two that the caretaker has not checked. I'll invite families only after six instruments pass. I will postpone the cello class and refund prepayments, not hand parents a repair bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you advertise with a pupil recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not use a child's rehearsal recording to promote the group without family permission. A live open rehearsal can show what pupils do without sending their voices into an advert.

say: I'd seek a **funded teacher certificate** that district schools accept.
I'd ask for **published school pay** before leaving current pupils.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I still need earnings for the mortgage.
**Film editing** may fade before 2036, while robot players follow around 2039.
do: Ask the **district** about an accepted certificate; enrol only with grant-covered fees and Jo covering childcare.
Aim for **one year saved** from spare paid lessons and shows after household bills before 2036.
Take a **posted school role** after 2036 only with signed net pay covering travel, mortgage and pickup; keep pupils until offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about earlier film-fee loss, though a funded route gives me time.
S4.quote: I would rather show my partner a funded course place than a hopeful leaflet.
fieldNote: Her **ten-year runway** supports a funded, district-recognised qualification while she keeps paid pupils and protects household savings.
Her **school move** requires a posted place, written net pay and workable child pickup.

steps.text: Check district certificate acceptance and grant before enrolling with Jo covering childcare
Aim for one year's reserve by 2036 from spare paid teaching/shows after household bills
Take posted school role after 2036 with written net-after-travel pay covering mortgage and pickup
Keep paid pupils until school offer and hours are signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players a decade is enough time to earn a teaching qualification, if the course and work are real. I would ask the district to publish the pay scale and funded places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I will still have a mortgage; robots able to play around 2039 could also reach the stage. Film editing may fade much sooner, so I want a steadier school wage without spending the children's reserve on a doubtful course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask whether the district accepts my bachelor's into its school-music certificate and whether a grant covers fees. I'll enrol only if a grant covers fees, Jo can cover the children's evenings and the district confirms the qualification. By 2036 I'll aim for a year's expenses saved from spare paid teaching and shows after household bills; in the first year after AGI, I'll take a posted school role only if written net pay after travel covers the mortgage and pickup, while keeping my paid pupils until the offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about film income slipping before 2036, but the longer runway helps. I would rather show my partner a funded course place than a hopeful leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the district accept that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A college course is not the same as district recognition. I will ask the district office directly before registering, and if it rejects the certificate I'll keep my present classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there actually a paid school place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school has no vacancy promised to me. Jo and I will compare the timetable with pickup and the written salary before changing my pupil list.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because studio fees could vanish before I have a different signed wage. Written orchestra hours, a genuinely open coach role and full lender costs if teaching falls would help us plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays when a loan cello fails during a children's class. A six-place class needs six safe instruments before six families are charged.

headlineQuote: A six-place class needs six safe instruments before six families are charged.
portrait: Uma is a **43-year-old cellist** with a music bachelor's, partner, two children and a mortgage.
Her **higher pay** and eight-month reserve let her negotiate, but studio preparation still matters.
She uses **AI daily** and checks new transcription against her own recordings.
She would pursue **paid teaching** and a funded district credential only with written terms.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could remove studio fees before another wage is signed.
whatWouldHelp: **Written orchestra hours**, a posted qualifying coach role and full lender costs would help her plan.
